'''Alexander Osipovich Gelfond''' ({{langx|ru|Алекса́ндр О́сипович Ге́льфонд}}; 24{{nbsp}}October 1906{{snd}}7{{nbsp}}November 1968) was a [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] mathematician. [[Gelfond–Schneider theorem|Gelfond's theorem]], also known as the Gelfond–Schneider theorem, is named after him.

==Biography==

Alexander Gelfond was born in Saint Petersburg, [[Russian Empire]], the son of a professional [[physician]] and amateur [[philosopher]] [[Osip Gelfond]].<ref name="Yandell">{{cite book |last1=Yandell |first1=Ben |title=The Honors Class: Hilbert's Problems and Their Solvers |date=2001 |publisher=CRC Press |location=Boca Ranton |isbn=9781439864227 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3UBZDwAAQBAJ&q=%22Osip+Gelfond%27&pg=PA192 |language=en}}</ref> He entered [[Moscow State University]] in 1924, started his postgraduate studies there in 1927, and obtained his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1930. His advisors were [[Aleksandr Khinchin]] (1894-1959) and [[Vyacheslav Stepanov]] (1889-1950).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Aleksandr Osipovich Gelfond - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Gelfond/ |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Aleksandr Gelfond - The Mathematics Genealogy Project |url=https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=56858 |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=www.mathgenealogy.org}}</ref>

In 1930, he stayed for five months in [[Germany]] (in [[Berlin]] and [[Göttingen]]) where he worked with [[Edmund Landau]], [[Carl Ludwig Siegel]], and [[David Hilbert]]. In 1931 he started teaching as a Professor at the Moscow State University and worked there until the last day of his life. Since 1933 he also worked at the [[Steklov Institute of Mathematics]].

In 1939, he was elected a [[Corresponding member]] of the [[Academy of Sciences of the Soviet Union]] for his works in the field of [[Cryptography]]. According to [[Vladimir Arnold]], during [[World War II]] Gelfond was the Chief Cryptographer of the [[Soviet Navy]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Arnold |first=Vladimir |script-title=ru:Владимир Арнольд: "Опасаться компетентных соперников очень естественно для начальников" |url=http://young-science.ru/sections/expertise/31-qq/1898-l-0q---.html |newspaper=[[Gazeta.ru]] |date=3 June 2006 |author-link=Vladimir Arnold |language=ru |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100610052252/http://www.gzt.ru/topnews/education/-vladimir-arnoljd-opasatjsya-kompetentnyh-/308825.html |archive-date=10 June 2010 |url-status=dead |access-date=10 August 2011 }}</ref>

==Results==
Gelfond obtained important results in several mathematical domains including [[number theory]], [[theory of analytic functions|analytic functions]], [[integral equation]]s, and the [[history of mathematics]], but his most famous result is his [[Gelfond's theorem|eponymous theorem]]:
{{block indent|1=If {{mvar|α}} and {{mvar|β}} are [[algebraic number]]s (with {{math|''α'' ≠ 0}} and {{math|''α'' ≠ 1}}), and if {{mvar|β}} is not a [[real number|real]] [[rational number]], then any value of {{math|''α''<sup>''β''</sup>}} is a [[transcendental number]].}}

This is the famous [[Hilbert's seventh problem|7th Hilbert's problem]]. Gelfond proved a special case of the theorem in 1929 when he was a postgraduate student and fully proved it in 1934. The same theorem was independently proven by [[Theodor Schneider]], and so the theorem is often known as the [[Gelfond–Schneider theorem]]. In 1929 Gelfond proposed an extension of the theorem known as  [[Gelfond's conjecture]] that was proven by [[Alan Baker (mathematician)|Alan Baker]] in 1966.

Before Gelfond's works only a few numbers such as {{mvar|[[E (mathematical constant)|e]]}} and [[Pi|{{pi}}]] were known to be transcendental. After his works, an infinite number of transcendentals could be easily obtained. Some of them are named in Gelfond's honor:
*{{math|2{{sup|{{sqrt|2}}}}}} is known as the [[Gelfond–Schneider constant]]
*{{math|''e''{{sup|''π''}}}} is known as [[Gelfond's constant]].
